clue.text: Sparks flying across centre in Montgenevre, before one social event there?

indicators.note: the scrambled group comes before the final piece in the answer
the scrambled letters stretch across the central letter, holding it inside them
sparks flying scatter in all directions, so the letters of the word are thrown into a new order
the centre of the long resort name is its middle letter

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Sparks fly at a French Alpine resort ahead of an evening's socialising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' scrambles SPARKS round E, the middle letter of Montgenevre, and I follows. Montgenevre is a ski resort, hence 'there?'.
explanation.definitionFit: The after-ski gathering is the social life that follows a day on the slopes at a resort.

clue.text: Summary difficult to understand

definitions.meaning: a short précis of an academic paper
theoretical and hard to grasp, not concrete

explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is a brief résumé of a paper; as an adjective, conceptual and hard to follow.

clue.text: Rule, then abdicate, not having son

indicators.note: not having means the letter is taken away from the word

parts.note: to abdicate is to resign the throne

explanation.surface: A monarch rules for a while and then steps down, being childless.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's period of sovereignty is their rule over the kingdom, a synonym.

clue.text: Description of a design that is second class

parts.note: a spec, short for specification, is a detailed description of a design
i.e., from Latin id est, means that is

explanation.surface: An account of a plan that turns out to be second-rate.
explanation.definitionFit: In biology a kind of organism is a class of living things, so the word means a type or category.

clue.text: Hold the fort?

definitions.meaning: to retain or hang on to
the central stronghold tower of a castle

explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to retain; as a noun it is a castle's strongest tower, a fortress within it.

clue.text: Notice only change

parts.note: an ad is a notice, an advertisement
just means only, as in just one

explanation.surface: An instruction that merely spotting something is enough to alter it.
explanation.definitionFit: To alter or modify something slightly is to make a small change to it, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Cover that's turned up on Austen novel causes a quandary

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means placed above the next piece
in a down clue turned up means the word is read from the bottom upwards, reversed

parts.note: a lid is a cover
Emma is a novel by Jane Austen

explanation.surface: A book jacket printed upside down on a Jane Austen classic creates a problem.
explanation.definitionFit: A difficult choice between two unsatisfactory options is a quandary, a synonym.

clue.text: Cinema worker is lax he utters — energy needs to be conserved

indicators.note: conserved means kept, so the letter is kept inside the rearranged letters
lax means loose, so the letters of the words are loosened into a new order

parts.note: E is the physics symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A lazy-tongued speaker is told to save his strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lax' rearranges HE UTTERS and E is put among those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who shows people to their seats in a picture house is a cinema employee.

clue.text: Reptile to go off, briefly let out

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: milk that goes off is said to turn

indicators.note: out means the letters of the word are put out of order

explanation.surface: Someone leaves quickly after being briefly released.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' shortens TURN to TUR; 'out' rearranges LET to TLE.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelled marine creature is a reptile, so this is an example of one.

clue.text: Yellow invertebrate?

definitions.meaning: yellow is slang for cowardly, lacking backbone
an invertebrate literally has no backbone, the query flagging the punning sense

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from lacking a backbone: figuratively timid, or literally without a spinal column.

clue.text: Jumped across opening in lane and caused a surprise

indicators.note: the word for jumped lies across the letter, enclosing it

parts.note: to have started is to have jumped with fright

indicators.note: the opening of the word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Something leapt over the start of a lane and gave someone a shock.
explanation.definitionFit: To have startled someone is to have given them a sudden shock, so it caused a surprise.

clue.text: Composer: he wrote nonsense about Hungary's capital

indicators.note: the writer's name goes about the letter, enclosing it

parts.note: Edward Lear was the Victorian writer of nonsense verse such as The Owl and the Pussy-cat

indicators.note: a capital letter here is the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A composer is said to have penned rubbish about Budapest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'he wrote nonsense' is not an anagram signal but a description of Edward Lear; Franz Lehar was a Hungarian composer of operettas.
explanation.definitionFit: Franz Lehar, writer of The Merry Widow, is an example of a composer of operetta.

clue.text: Bad storm around northern end of Quebec

indicators.note: the raid goes around the two letters, enclosing them

parts.note: to storm a place is to raid it

indicators.note: the end of the word is its last letter

explanation.surface: A violent storm sweeps around the northern tip of Quebec.
explanation.definitionFit: Food that is rancid has gone off, so it is bad in the sense of spoiled.

clue.text: Healing ointment said to come from a royal residence

parts.note: balm is a soothing healing ointment
oral means spoken, said rather than written

explanation.surface: A soothing cream reputedly comes from one of the King's homes.
explanation.walkthrough: Balmoral is the royal family's castle in Aberdeenshire, Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish castle is a home of the British monarch, an example of a royal residence.

clue.text: Great local's so in need of renovation

indicators.note: renovation means the letters are rebuilt into a new order

parts.note: the possessive s is used as a letter here

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that the neighbourhood pub is badly run down.
explanation.walkthrough: The S of local's counts as a letter in the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something huge or enormous is great in size, a synonym.

clue.text: English inside eat hot scones prepared as a snack

indicators.note: the single letter goes inside the rearranged letters
the words are prepared, made up into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Advice to eat warm scones, made ready as a light bite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eat hot scones prepared' reads as a recipe, but 'prepared' is the anagram signal and the snack is the toasted cheese dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Melted cheddar on grilled bread is a classic light British meal, an example of a snack.

clue.text: Relaxed, getting simple summons to meal about lunchtime?

parts.note: easy means simple

indicators.note: the gong goes about the numeral, enclosing it

parts.note: a gong is struck to summon people to a meal
lunch is at one o'clock, and I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A laid-back diner hears the lunch gong and drifts in.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who is calm and unflustered is laid-back, relaxed.

clue.text: The sort of stale joke that might get a roasting!

definitions.text: The sort of stale joke that might get a roasting!

parts.words: The sort of stale joke that might get a roasting!
parts.note: an old tired joke is called an old ..., and the nut of that name is roasted on an open fire

explanation.definitionFit: A hackneyed joke is known by the name of a nut that is traditionally roasted in winter.

clue.text: Threaten to turn up with broken nose and choppers

parts.note: to show is to turn up, arrive

indicators.note: broken means the letters of the word are smashed into a new order

parts.note: choppers is slang for teeth

explanation.surface: Someone arrives with a smashed nose and missing teeth, looking menacing.
explanation.definitionFit: Baring the fangs is an idiom for making a menacing display, so it means to threaten.

clue.text: Her opus excited entrancing poet

indicators.note: excited means the letters of the words are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: Her musical work thrilled a spellbinding versifier.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary Greek singer charmed beasts and the underworld with his lyre, a poet who entranced.

clue.text: Rough terrain for a coach

indicators.note: rough means the letters of the word are roughed up into a new order

explanation.surface: Bumpy ground suitable for a long-distance bus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coach' suggests a bus on rough roads; it is a sports coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports trainer instructs athletes, so this is a synonym for a coach.

clue.text: Published, and gets prosecuted?

definitions.meaning: brought out, as a book or statement
read as two words, is taken to court, with the query flagging the split

explanation.definitionFit: It means brought out in print; split into two words it says someone is taken to court.

clue.text: One may help you along the way

definitions.text: One may help you along the way

parts.words: One may help you along the way
parts.note: the surface suggests a kindly helper; the thing meant points travellers along the road

explanation.definitionFit: A roadside pointer shows travellers the direction to take, helping them along their route.

clue.text: Caught, sadly, bringing in illegal, originally from ferry port

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught

indicators.note: the word for sadly brings in the letter, holding it inside

parts.note: alas is an exclamation said sadly

indicators.note: originally means the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is caught, regrettably, smuggling contraband off a cross-Channel boat.
explanation.definitionFit: The French town is a major Channel crossing point, an example of a ferry port.

clue.text: A nearly new suit

indicators.note: nearly means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: green means new, inexperienced

explanation.surface: An almost brand-new outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'suit' is the verb, as in 'that suits me'.
explanation.definitionFit: To suit someone is to be acceptable to them, as in 'that date will agree with me'.

clue.text: First to sell meat paste?

indicators.note: first to means the first letter of the word

parts.note: ham is a meat

explanation.surface: The top item to sell is meat spread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'paste' suggests a meat spread, but paste is imitation gemstone, a fake.
explanation.definitionFit: Paste is glass made to imitate gems, so it is a fake or sham.

clue.text: Join one by end of esplanade

indicators.note: by means next to, so the letter is placed beside the word

parts.note: a unit is one, a single thing

indicators.note: the end of the word is its last letter

explanation.surface: An invitation to meet up beside the far end of the seafront promenade.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring together or combine things is to join them, a plain synonym.

clue.text: Wagner opera long confused with Rhine

indicators.note: confused means the letters of the two words are mixed up together

explanation.surface: A Wagner work that drags on gets muddled with his Rhine operas.
explanation.definitionFit: The swan-knight opera of 1850 is one of Wagner's best-known works, an example.

clue.text: Synopsis to think over

definitions.meaning: a summary or condensed account of a text
to absorb and reflect on information

explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is a condensed summary; as a verb, to ponder and take something in mentally.

clue.text: Budding team up in hospital unit

indicators.note: the word for team up goes in the hospital department

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital
to merge is to team up, combine

explanation.surface: Promising young players join forces on a hospital ward.
explanation.definitionFit: Something just coming into being is emerging or developing, like a bud about to open.
